client: I've been really stressed out lately because I missed the deadline for my final project at university, and I honestly can't stop thinking about how badly it's going to affect my grade. Every time I sit down to try and work on it now, I just freeze up and feel this wave of panic wash over me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the damage is kind of already done, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now — the stress of the missed deadline, the freezing up, and even some doubt about whether this conversation can help. I notice that as you're describing all of this, there's something almost quiet and withdrawn in the way you're speaking, even though the situation feels so overwhelming inside — I'm wondering if part of you is feeling more defeated or exhausted than panicked right now? Sometimes when we've been running on anxiety for a while, we can reach a point of emotional exhaustion that feels different from the initial panic — does that resonate with you at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, that actually does resonate more than I expected it to. It's like the panic was loud at first, but now I just feel... flat, almost numb about the whole thing with the deadline and my boss probably thinking I can't handle my job. I'm not sure if that's better or worse than the panic, honestly.
therapist: That shift from panic to numbness makes a lot of sense — it's like your mind has been running so hard that it's hit a kind of protective wall, and yet I'm noticing something interesting: the way you're speaking carries a kind of energy that feels almost brighter than the flatness you're describing, like there's still something very much alive and stirred up underneath that numbness. I'm also curious — you mentioned your boss now, which is a new piece of the picture — is the worry about work something that's been tangled up in this stress all along, or is that a separate weight you've been carrying quietly on top of everything else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, the work stuff has definitely been tangled up in all of this the whole time, I just... I don't know, I guess I kept pushing it to the side because it felt almost too stressful to even bring up. My boss has been making these little comments lately, like implying I'm not pulling my weight, and every time it happens I just freeze up and then spend the rest of the day replaying it in my head wondering if she's right. And honestly, maybe that's part of why I feel so numb — like I've been carrying this quiet dread about my job on top of everything else, and at some point my brain just said "enough."
therapist: It takes real courage to bring that into the open, and it sounds like you've been quietly managing so much more than just the deadline — that constant replaying of your boss's comments, wondering if she's right, is such an exhausting place to live in your head. What stands out to me is that word you used: *maybe she's right* — I'm curious, when you hear that thought, does it feel like a fact to you, or more like a fear that's been growing louder the more stressed and stretched you've become?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, in the moment it feels like a fact — like, my brain just accepts it as true without me even questioning it. But when you put it that way, asking if it's a fear that's gotten louder... I don't know, maybe there's something to that, because it does seem to get worse when I'm already exhausted or behind on things. It's just hard to separate the two when I'm in the middle of it.
therapist: What you just noticed is actually really significant — that the thought feels loudest and most like "truth" precisely when you're already running on empty, which is such an important clue that it might be exhaustion and stress doing the talking, not an accurate reflection of your abilities. In CBT, we call these kinds of automatic thoughts — ones that feel like facts but are actually shaped by our emotional state — and the fact that you can already see the pattern is the first step toward being able to catch them in the moment. I'm wondering, can you think of any evidence from your work or university life that might push back against the idea that you're not pulling your weight — even something small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... I guess there was that group project last semester where my professor actually pulled me aside to say my research section was really thorough. But it's hard to hold onto that because it feels like a long time ago, and right now all I can think about is how behind I am on everything. It's like the good stuff just... doesn't stick the same way the bad stuff does.
therapist: That example about your professor is really worth holding onto — it's real, it happened, and it says something genuine about your capabilities that your exhausted brain is currently trying to talk you out of. What you're describing, where the negative stuff sticks like velcro and the positive slides right off, is actually one of the most common patterns we see in anxiety and burnout, and it means your mind has been filtering the evidence unfairly against you for a while now. I'm curious — what do you think it would feel like to deliberately keep a small record of moments like that professor's comment, not to force positivity, but just to give your brain a fairer set of evidence to work with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like yeah, my brain is probably being unfair to me. But honestly, the idea of keeping some kind of record feels a little... forced? Like I'd be writing things down just to convince myself of something, and I'm not sure I'd even believe it when I read it back.
therapist: That hesitation makes complete sense, and I don't want to push you toward something that feels hollow — if it doesn't feel genuine, it probably won't help much. What I'm noticing though is that even as you're pushing back on the idea, you're speaking quite quickly, like there's something a little charged or unsettled in how you're engaging with it — I wonder if part of you is less "this won't work" and more "I'm scared it still won't be enough to quiet that critical voice"? What do you think is underneath the doubt — is it more that the exercise feels artificial, or more that you're not sure you deserve to believe the good evidence even when it's right in front of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hate that you noticed that, because you're probably right. It's not really that the exercise feels fake — it's more like, even if I gather all this evidence that I'm a decent person, there's still this voice that just... dismisses it, like it doesn't count or I'm just fooling myself. And I think deep down I'm scared that no amount of evidence is ever going to be enough to actually convince me, so why even try.
therapist: What you just said took real courage, and I want to sit with it for a moment — because naming that fear, that "why even try," is actually one of the most honest and important things you've shared so far. That dismissive inner voice you're describing isn't a sign that the evidence is wrong or that you're fooling yourself; it sounds like a voice that's been around for a long time, maybe long before the deadline or your boss's comments, and it's worth gently exploring where it came from. Can I ask — does that voice remind you of anything or anyone familiar, or does it feel like something that's always just been part of how you see yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, actually. Now that you're asking, it does remind me of something — my dad used to say stuff like "don't get too excited, you'll just disappoint yourself," almost like a warning every time I tried something new. I guess I never really connected that to how I talk to myself at work, but sitting here right now, it feels kind of obvious and also kind of... heavy.
therapist: That connection you just made is profound, and I can hear how much weight it carries — your dad's words were meant to protect you, maybe, but what they also did was plant that dismissive voice so early and so deep that it started to feel like your own. It makes so much sense that it's followed you into how you judge yourself at work and university, because we often internalize the voices of the people who raised us without even realizing it. I want to ask gently — as you sit with that realization right now, what does it feel like to see that voice as something that was given to you, rather than something that's simply the truth about who you are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: It's... strange, actually. Like, part of me wants to feel relieved by that idea, that it's not just the truth about me, but another part keeps pushing back and saying "well, what if your dad was right, what if he just saw something real that you still can't admit?" I don't know how to separate what's actually true about me from what he put there, because it's been so long that it all feels like the same thing.
therapist: The fact that those two things have blurred together over so many years — his voice and your own — makes it genuinely hard to know where one ends and the other begins, and that confusion is completely understandable. But I want to gently point something out: the part of you that *wants* to feel relieved, that reached toward the idea that this isn't simply the truth about you — that part is also real, and it's been quietly fighting for you this whole conversation. I'm wondering, if you tried to imagine a close friend describing you the way your dad's voice describes you, would it feel like truth, or would something in you want to push back on their behalf?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: If a close friend said those things to me, yeah, I'd probably want to defend them. I'd think, no, that's not fair, you're being too hard on yourself. But when I try to turn that same instinct toward myself, it just... doesn't work the same way, like there's some wall that goes up and says "no, but in your case it actually is true."
therapist: That wall you're describing — the one that makes an exception for you specifically — is one of the most telling things you've said, because it means you already *have* the capacity for compassion and fairness, you just have a deeply ingrained rule that says you don't qualify for it. That rule didn't come from evidence, it came from a little kid who learned to agree with a parent's voice in order to make sense of the world. What would it mean for you — even just as an experiment — to treat that wall not as the truth, but as the oldest, most stubborn thought distortion you've ever had to work with?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
